title: When nutrition means more than food - University of New Hampshire
content: Several UNH Extension programs are demonstrating that meeting the nutritional needs of neighbors can also build community, improve efficiency and effectiveness, and promote a feeling of dignity. A couple of years ago an elementary class in Berlin, New Hampshire, reached out to an Extension educator for help with a class gardening project. A grandparent of one of the students heard about it and asked if Extension could help start a vegetable plot at their senior living facility. And then a food pantry wanted to know if they could grow some produce in an underused city park next door. What’s blossomed since then is not just vegetable plants but a sense of togetherness: Neighbors and friends work together to plan and tend gardens, a shared resource that provides both sustenance and social well-being. Mandy Bernd is a steward with the Community Builders Hub, a nonprofit that fosters collaborative problem-solving and is one of several local organizations that has joined the garden project. She says the project is succeeding because of an element that’s hard to measure but would be noticeable if absent. “We bring the fun,” Bernd says. “It’s not just ‘Come with a shovel.’ It’s also ‘Let’s have lunch together.’ We have music blasting; this year we have kids coming with their parents, too.” The newest garden is in Friendship Park, on the corner of Granite and Mason streets. Cindy Lapointe, recently retired, was the program director for day services at Northern Human Services, an organization that assists people with disabilities. She says she agreed to help start the gardens last year despite her initial doubts. “We did not think this was going to work; there were too many barriers,” Lapointe says. There was no water at the park, the garden boxes were dilapidated, and nobody knew how they were going to organize labor. But Zeanny Egea Alvarado, then the Extension educator working in Berlin, brought an infectious kind of optimism. Someone at City Hall knew how to get new garden boxes built. A contractor donated a cistern for watering, and the fire department agreed to keep it filled. Several other people joined in their own ways, such as building adapters so hoses could be fitted to the cistern or donating seedlings they had grown at home. “Everybody just pitched in. It was fantastic,” Lapointe says, noting that on some days there are more than 30 visitors from various organizations and from the neighborhood, all brought together by the shared project. The Feeding Hope Food Pantry was one of the first organizations to join the garden project. Director Sarah Swift says she was motivated by a desire to see her clients eat less canned food and more fresh vegetables. “The fact that prices have all gone up makes it more difficult for people to get fresh produce,” she says, noting the excitement that shoppers at her pantry showed about the availability of crisp vegetables. “They were surprised, because they didn’t know anybody would do this kind of thing in the community. But when they found out we were doing it in a local public park, that’s what really stirred their interest.” Swift says that many of her clients are elderly or disabled, or for other reasons might not feel capable of growing a garden alone. But many of them have the capability to help. “The volunteers I have, they really feel connected,” Swift says. “They like to feel that they’re providing [food] as well as benefiting from it. They feel like they’re helping provide for other people. It’s the power to help. It’s knowing that they can be a part of the help, too.” Operating a food pantry is challenging in many ways, and one of those ways is helping people who have had a complicated relationship with food. They might have limited experience with certain ingredients, chronic health problems that are tied to diet, or trauma related to food insecurity. The Nutritious Pantry Program, a menu of services provided by Extension, is there to help. Several pantries have engaged in the program, each identifying an area in which they’d like to improve. One participating pantry is Twin Rivers in Franklin, which serves 16 communities and around 800 families each month, according to its director, Alison Jones. “Extension helped us reimagine our pantry,” Jones says. “It’s very expansive, this program. We’ve been The partnership with Twin Rivers started with a survey of shoppers, which resulted in some easy changes, such as providing water for shoppers during the warm months and adding margarine to the butter case. But it also revealed just how many of them were living with cardiac disease, diabetes, or other conditions that put higher stakes on their eating habits. With that information in hand, the food pantry began sharing its expected deliveries with Extension, which responded with healthy recipes that use those ingredients. The pantry often prepares those dishes and provides samples to shoppers, who can also take a copy of the recipe home if they like it. The Extension recipes are collected in a pantry cookbook that is given to new families. There are changes visible inside the pantry, too. Twin Rivers now has electronic display monitors and clearer signage for shoppers looking for low-salt and low-sugar foods. During the growing season, the pantry accesses grant funds to buy directly from local farmers. Swift says she’s proud of what her pantry has become. “A woman in her 60s, who came back to get more fresh vegetables, said she had never eaten healthier in her life,” Swift says. “We are making a real impact on the health and well-being of our shoppers.” Across the state, food access networks are either starting up or getting organized. In both cases, they are intended to replicate the structure and efficacy of the Carroll County Food Access Network (CCFAN), which Joy Gagnon, an Extension educator on the Food and Agriculture Team, started several years ago. Gagnon works in Carroll County, a large geographic area filled with small towns. It’s a county marked by rural beauty, recreation hubs, and pockets of isolation and poverty. The CCFAN was needed because local assistance for those struggling with hunger was often as isolated as the clientele, unconnected to or unaware of similar efforts happening in the next town or valley. Gagnon started attempting to organize the network during the COVID pandemic, but she encountered an initial reluctance. She established momentum in 2023 after completing a needs assessment. She interviewed all the agencies she thought should be part of the network, compiled the results, and then returned the results to the individual agencies. The data clearly showed that problems in one community were also encountered by their neighbors, and that dozens of small organizations were struggling with a common challenge. “That’s what inspired a lot of participation in the group,” Gagnon explains. Some of her member agencies consist of just a handful of local volunteers, while others are school districts or hospital organizations. “It’s a network of at least 25 organizations working together to solve the issue of food access,” she says. Members are kept engaged, Gagnon says, because CCFAN is focused on goals and results. Each year, goals are established and the members organize around the specific objectives that make sense to their organization’s mission and capabilities. Sometimes, surprising partnerships emerge. In one such example, the New Hampshire Food Bank was setting up its yearly effort to provide food for schoolchildren during the summer. As part of CCFAN, they were in a working group with Tri-County Transit, which offered to provide delivery as an option for participating families. That collaboration led to a tenfold increase in participation, because the Food Bank started reaching families that didn’t have the means to travel to a weekly distribution point. Heidi Johnson, SNAP outreach and application assistance senior coordinator for the New Hampshire Food Bank, says the success of CCFAN is due to its champion: “Joy is well organized and a very good leader, pulling together the necessary people to identify and focus on the priorities in the area. She’s an inspiration to the members and a model for other regional coalitions.” Considered together, these programs show that the work of nutrition access means more than distribution of food, says Amy Hollar, state specialist and professor of nutrition and food access for Extension. “Extension's nutrition and food access initiatives are increasing access to fresh, healthy, local food, but they are also doing more than that — our programs stimulate community conversations and strengthen relationships,” Hollar says. “If we want to eliminate a complex, social issue like hunger in NH, we need whole communities working together. This is how Extension approaches our nutrition  and food access work: By bringing a community together to grow a garden, by guiding a food pantry to learn from and respond to their guests, and by creating and sustaining communication and support systems that enable community coalitions to act together to ensure that everyone has a fair and just opportunity to be as healthy as possible.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: Cash Crab - University of New Hampshire
content: In 2018, when the first Green Crab Working Summit was held, it was an attempt by researchers at UNH Extension, NH Sea Grant and Manomet Conservation Sciences to inspire an industry around the harvesting and processing of an invasive species. By the time the second summit was held in Portland, Maine, in June 2026, that industry was alive and growing. The emergence of the industry has been a robust validation of that first summit, which was organized by UNH Extension and New Hampshire Sea Grant in partnership with Manomet Conservation Sciences. Green crabs, native to Europe, have been seen on the Eastern Seaboard since at least 1817 but warming waters have been pushing them steadily northward. The goal of summit organizers was to come up with a way to make use of the crabs. In doing so, they hoped to relieve some of the pressure the crabs are placing on native species and slow down the ecological and economic damage that they were causing. “When I started, nobody was doing anything with them,” recalls Gabriela Bradt, fisheries and aquaculture specialist for UNH Extension and NH Sea Grant, who along with Marissa McMahan from Manomet Conservation has been pioneering the green crab industry in New England. “Harvesters are actively targeting these crabs and selling them; people are beginning to start businesses and making products out of them. It’s on people’s radar much more than it ever had been.” The first Green Crab Summit, held in 2018, was held to showcase and characterize the research done to that point and establish connections and working partnerships. For the second summit, the focus was turned to the industry that the research enabled. Mary Parks helped organize the initial summit and her organization, GreenCrab.org, which she founded in 2020, was one of the hosts, along with Extension, NH Sea Grant, and Manomet, for this year’s summit. “A lot of people are working with green crabs, not just because they see an ecological value in removing them from the ecosystem but because of the culinary value,” says Parks. She adds that between 2020 and 2025, the number of restaurants around the country that have served green crab at least once increased twelvefold to 112. There can be a bit of a learning curve for Western-trained chefs, as green crabs are smaller than those that North American restaurants typically serve. However, in southern Europe, where green crabs are native, and in Southeast Asia, where there are other crabs of similar size, small crustaceans are prized for use in fish sauces and powdered broths, or as the base for a bisque. Several businesses in New England have learned from those traditions to add to their own product lines, Parks notes. Meanwhile, Bradt’s research has led to new ways to use the crab, such as in fertilizer, fish sauce, eaten whole while its shell is soft, or even in a whiskey. Bradt says the goal isn’t eradication, as that isn’t feasible in the Northeast. Instead, she hopes the industry can remove enough green crabs to give local species a chance to protect their own populations. The work of researchers continues, with the goal of finding yet more ways to entice enterprise. Bradt founded and leads the NH Green Crab Project, which began with basic ecological and biological research and now includes market and fishery development. The project includes the Great Green Crab Hunt, a participatory science program that invites members of the public to help track the crab population. “We started out with nothing, NH Sea Grant/Extension and Manomet have been instrumental in market and fishery creation, business development, and industry support and bringing the necessary stakeholders to the table,” says Bradt. “People are trying to figure out how to take it further.” Parks says there is now an industry full of people with vested interests in serving green crabs. She remembers when it was just a few people with a big idea. Now it’s a growing industry, thanks to the innovation and collaboration of hard-working partners. Parks says, “It’s so important that we have collaboration between chefs and culinary organizations and the research community. That’s the power of organizations that can work across these groups.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: Durham Reacts to Two New Restaurant Chains - The New Hampshire
content: DURHAM — On Sept. 23, Chipotle Mexican Grill officially opened its doors at 7 Mill Road in Durham, New Hampshire, marking the second national restaurant chain to make its local debut. Next door, Jersey Mike’s is approaching its third month of business in Durham. The arrival of both chains has generated excitement among UNH students, who now have two new dining options and potential employers close to campus. “I was really excited for the two new stores to open when I heard about it. I’m a big fan of Chipotle, and I am excited to go in Durham,” said James Reda, a senior at UNH, describing his initial reaction to the restaurants’ arrival. These new Durham locations will affect more than UNH students. Their arrival raises questions about competition, convenience and employment in a college town where local restaurants have long been part of the community. “The general consensus that we’ve heard from other business owners is that Durham had really resisted this type of business for a long time, and so a lot of people were really disappointed,” said Erin McGinley, co-owner of JP’s Grill. McGinley and her husband, Michael, bought JP’s Grill in 2018. Since then, the restaurant has become a downtown dining staple for students and residents alike. “I’d be lying if I said we weren’t disappointed,” McGinley said, describing the restaurant’s initial reaction to news of the new chains. McGinley said larger companies have a potential advantage when it comes to marketing and advertising, resources that smaller businesses often struggle to match. “You’re not going to see a JP’s logo on the ice rink, for example,” McGinley said. Like McGinley, Kim Clark, owner of Clark’s American Bistro on Main Street in Durham, shares concerns about the marketing capabilities of larger chains. Clark’s has been a family-owned establishment for over 100 years. “We are hopeful that the local community will still be interested in conducting dine and donate with us, but do wonder if their [Chipotle and Jersey Mike's] ability to market at a corporate level may impact this,” Clark said. Clark was referring to her restaurant’s weekly Dine and Donate/We Care Wednesdays, where 10% of food sales are donated to a local cause. She is also the director of business of practice and a lecturer of management at UNH. Across the street from JP’s Grill and Clark’s American Bistro, Pauly’s Pockets has also been family-owned for over 20 years right here in Durham. “This business, Mom and Pop, it’s gonna die, sooner or later,” said Paul Eja, owner of Pauly’s Pockets. “It’s a good business to be in a college town, but not like how it used to be,” Eja said. Eja sees several benefits to operating a business in a college town, including new students arriving each year, extra-busy semester periods and proximity to campus. However, he also pointed to some of the downsides of running a business in Durham. “We used to do business from 9 o’clock in the morning, the next day 3-4 o’clock in the morning. Nonstop. Then the new dining hall came onboard, and took a lot of business from Main Street,” Eja said. Like McGinley and Clark, Eja believes the new restaurants will benefit the community, even as they bring more competition to local businesses. “Good for Durham, good for students, I’m not against it, but it will take more business,” Eja said. While small businesses prepare to compete with the new establishments, students have already started digging in, and some are cashing in. “So far it has been good, I like my coworkers, everyone who works there goes to UNH so it’s been fun,” said Bella Esposito, a junior at UNH who has worked at Chipotle since its opening on September 23. Esposito has found that the majority of Chipotle’s customers are students, and lots of them. “There’s been a lot of people, and there have been days where we ran out of stuff. I worked the last tailgate and it was crazy,” Esposito said. The buzz around campus is real, as students routinely trek down to Mast Road to indulge in Durham’s latest offerings. “Only time will tell,” McGinley said, reflecting on the future of Durham’s local restaurant scene as Chipotle and Jersey Mike’s establish themselves in town.

title: Chris Pappas Visits UNH, and Encourages Students to Vote Ahead of November Election - The New Hampshire
content: DURHAM, N.H. – U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas, D-N.H., visited the University of New Hampshire on Tuesday, Oct. 20, encouraging students to register to vote and discussing issues affecting younger generations ahead of the Nov. 3 general election. During his visit, Pappas walked through the Memorial Union Building (MUB), speaking with students about the upcoming election and the importance of political participation. He also stopped by the UNH Student Senate room, where he spoke with student representatives. Pappas, who currently represents New Hampshire's 1st Congressional District, is running for the U.S. Senate against Republican John E. Sununu. With Election Day just two weeks away, Pappas emphasized the importance of engaging younger voters and ensuring their concerns are represented in Washington. When asked why he chose to visit UNH, Pappas said he wanted to support voter registration efforts and encourage students to participate in the upcoming election. "We want to support the effort, you know, in terms of making sure people register, and have their voices heard in November," Pappas said. "It's a great campus." Throughout his visit, Pappas spoke about the role younger generations play in shaping the country's political future, arguing that students should not wait until later in life to become involved in politics. "There are people counting your generation out, people that are just trying to protect things the way that they are right now," Pappas said. Pappas argued that the current economic and political system benefits wealthy Americans and large corporations while leaving younger generations to deal with rising costs and financial uncertainty. "The status quo is working well for the corporation, for the wealthiest Americans. But what about the things that are falling on your shoulders in terms of how this economy isn't functioning, issues like housing and higher education affordability," Pappas said. Pappas encouraged students to recognize their ability to influence political decisions, particularly on issues that will affect their futures. "I’ve got to make sure that you all feel empowered to have your voice heard and sort of take control of our democracy," Pappas said. "We can't wait 20 or 30 years for that to happen. It needs to happen now." Beyond voter participation, Pappas addressed the financial challenges facing college students in New Hampshire, including the cost of higher education, housing and everyday expenses. When asked what he believes is the biggest concern facing college students in New Hampshire and how he would address it if elected to the Senate, Pappas pointed to affordability as a major issue. "The cost of everything's way too high, and whether that is tuition, housing, or just everything people need in their day-to-day lives, it's been going up over the last couple years," Pappas said. He emphasized the need for greater investment in education at both the state and federal levels, arguing that students should not have to carry the financial burden of rising costs without additional support. "UNH is last in the nation in terms of state support for education. So we’ve got to do better at the state level and the federal level too," Pappas said. He also discussed the need to lower the cost of gas, health care and housing, connecting these concerns to broader political issues in Washington. "We have to bring down the cost of gas and healthcare and housing, all the things that people need to live successful lives," Pappas said. Pappas criticized the current administration and what he described as a lack of accountability in Washington, arguing that changes in congressional leadership are necessary to address everyday concerns. "I'm really worried about where we are as a country. We've got no checks and balances in Washington right now, and a president that is totally incompetent every day," Pappas said. "So we got to stand up and demand better, and restore an ability to get things done and focus on people's day-to-day lives." When asked what sets him apart from his Republican opponent, former U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu, particularly when it comes to representing younger generations, Pappas pointed to Sununu's previous record in Washington. "He went to Washington 30 years ago. He has been a congressman, he's been a senator before," Pappas said. Pappas criticized Sununu's positions on reproductive rights, Social Security and the invasion in Iraq arguing that New Hampshire should not return to what he described as a failed political history. "That's part of a failed political history that we shouldn't have to go back to," Pappas said. "This should be about how we write a different chapter for the future." Pappas contrasted Sununu's record with his own experience representing New Hampshire and his priorities if elected to the Senate. "I have a small business background. I've been fighting hard the last few years to expand access to healthcare, to protect our environment, to protect reproductive freedom, to make sure that we're investing in education," Pappas said. "Those are fights that I want to take to the Senate." He argued that the election represents a choice between maintaining the current direction of the federal government and changing the balance of power in Washington. "I'm on the side of shaking up the status quo and making our political system function for everyday Americans and Granite Staters," Pappas said. With Election Day approaching, Pappas also shared his message for voters who remain undecided. "This is an election where we can deliver change if people are willing to speak out," Pappas said. He pointed to political dysfunction, economic inequality and the influence of wealthy individuals and corporations as reasons voters should become involved. "It doesn't have to be this way, and if people of good conscience get engaged and decide to vote, we can take the power of our democracy in our own hands," Pappas said. Pappas emphasized the importance of restoring checks and balances in Washington and changing the balance of power in the Senate. "We need to restore checks and balances in Washington and flip the majority in the U.S. Senate, so that we have some guardrails for the American people, and that we can get back down to business to solve problems again," Pappas said. He added that representing New Hampshire should involve addressing the needs of people across different generations, including students, families and older residents. "New Hampshire's a great state, there's a lot going for us. There are challenges here, and this should be about how we focus on the needs of students and families and seniors, and, you know, just make sure that everyone's heard," Pappas said. While much of his visit focused on the upcoming election, Pappas stressed that political engagement should continue beyond November. "It's not about just winning one election. It's how you build progress over time," Pappas said. "Because there are no permanent victories or defeats in our political system. You gotta keep people engaged."

title: For a Growing Number of Companies, UNH Is Home - University of New Hampshire
content: Olson Center Director John Roth, Airtho President Brandon Bogart, and N.H. Governor Kelly Ayotte at the dedication of Airtho's new cleanroom at the Olson Center. When Airtho, a New Hampshire-based controlled environments developer, outgrew its office, it moved to a new yet familiar location: UNH. For several years, Airtho had worked with UNH’s John Olson Advanced Manufacturing Center on product development and testing, and half of its employees were UNH alumni. In 2022, Airtho co-located its growing business with the Olson Center. “Moving to UNH has given me a more accessible pool of talented people and that has helped me grow the business pretty significantly,” says Airtho President Brandon Bogart, adding that the company has doubled its revenue year-over-year since co-locating. Airtho’s success is hardly an outlier. A dozen companies currently co-locate at UNH in Durham, a 400% increase since 2022, and more are in the wings. “UNH’s resources and reputation are attracting business and industry innovators to campus and the local area, who in turn generate economic benefits for the entire state of New Hampshire,” says Jennifer Miksis-Olds, interim vice president of research and innovation. “Partners are coming to us from across the state and around the globe to access our state-of-the-art facilities, research expertise, and students.” Miksis-Olds was the founding director of UNH’s Center for Acoustics Research and Education, which is a key collaborator with UNH’s most recent co-locator: defense technology and software company Integer Technologies. Integer established a presence in Conant Hall in spring 2026 to develop advanced acoustic technologies that enhance U.S. Navy capabilities. “Through this partnership with UNH, we are helping to advance the understanding of how sound behaves in the ocean while strengthening the specialized workforce needed to develop technology and apply that understanding in support of critical missions,” says Integer CEO and co-founder Duke Hartman. For most industry partners, UNH’s facilities resources are the initial draw. Johnny’s Selected Seeds lacks sophisticated climate-controlled greenhouses like UNH’s Macfarlane Research Greenhouses. “We have high tunnels, like farmers,” says Johnny’s Vice President of Research and Development Kevin Cook, referring to the unheated plastic-covered structures, but not a space to grow and develop a new, disease-resistant variety of cut zinnias in the winter, when they’re less busy. What’s more, UNH professor emeritus Tom Davis and his Ph.D. student Mamta Kajal are doing the very specific breeding research that’s likely to yield the zinnias Johnny’s hopes to produce. “This expertise is basically in our backyard,” says Cook. “Very quickly we came to understand that [students] provide a fantastic opportunity for us. Without them, we wouldn’t have been able to do what we’ve done, which has helped us advance several drug discovery programs.” Laboratory facilities are what drew RexChem founder Mark Spyvee, a longtime New Hampshire resident, to UNH after his company outgrew its incubator space in Massachusetts. He found his way to UNH, where RexChem shares lab space with professor of chemistry Erik Berda. “Very quickly we came to understand that [students] provide a fantastic opportunity for us,” says Spyvee, who has hired nine undergraduates since RexChem has been at UNH. “Without them, we wouldn’t have been able to do what we’ve done, which has helped us advance several drug discovery programs.” The collaboration benefits the students, too. “Essentially they have been doing what a professional chemist would do,” Spyvee says: gaining on-the-job skills, networking with industry, and pursuing research that has a real impact are among the benefits co-locating partners offer students. Two trade organizations also call UNH home. The New Hampshire Manufacturing Extension Partnership (NH MEP), a public-private partnership that provides resources to Granite State manufacturers, recently moved its primary office to the Olson Center. And the trade consortium New Hampshire Aerospace and Defense Consortium (NHADC) has found UNH Manchester to be the ideal hub from which to connect manufacturing, government, and education. The Queen City location puts NHADC at the center of the state’s manufacturing ecosystem, and it also helps NHADC leverage student talent. “Being able to directly connect our students with our membership is really important,” says NHADC Director Randy Makee ‘09G, who also teaches a course in operations management at UNH Manchester. In July, UNH hosted U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen and others at a beam-signing ceremony for a 70,500-square foot building that will house the Center of Excellence for Operational Ocean and Great Lakes Mapping and co-location space for industry partners. The facility, on the edge of the UNH campus, is expected to open in 2027. Mamta Kajal, a Ph.D. student in professor emeritus Tom Davis's lab, is working with Johnny's Selected Seeds to develop a new variety of zinnia seeds. Co-location has brought some unexpected benefits to industry. RexChem utilizes some of the extremely expensive shared equipment in the University Instrumentation Center, nearby in Parsons Hall. title: What's it like to study biomedical science at UNH? A pre-vet student shares her experience - University of New Hampshire
content: Meet Laurabeth Bestwick, a junior biomedical science major on the pre-veterinary track at the University of New Hampshire. Laurabeth shares how a challenging organic chemistry course became an unexpected favorite, what she's learned through hands-on animal anatomy courses, and how UNH is preparing her for a future as an equine veterinarian and surgeon. I chose UNH because of its many research opportunities and beautiful campus. I felt welcomed by the faculty and staff when I toured as a freshman and knew I had to enroll. I would tell my freshman self to leave her comfort zone and try new things! All my favorite things about my college experience so far, is the result of introducing myself to people or trying new activities. My favorite UNH course so far has been Environment and Society taught by Cliff Brown. I loved our many discussions about contemporary political, social, and ethical issues. Dr. Brown was very passionate about his class and that enthusiasm was infectious. I chose Biomedical Science because its required courses that will prepare me for veterinary school post-graduation. I wanted a science-based major with lots of opportunities for laboratory work and hands-on experience, which this major has given me. I've found a wonderful sense of community amongst my fellow pre-vet students, who understand both the stress and joy that our courses give us. My entire experience in organic chemistry stands out to me. I was very nervous to take that class and ended up enjoying it more than I ever thought I would. It was very difficult, and I had to work hard to succeed, but I proved to myself that I was capable of the discipline and effort necessary to excel in a challenging course. The dissections I completed in my Animal Anatomy & Physiology course were all very impactful and important to my learning. Getting to see real-life versions of the things we learned about in class gave me another level of understanding that I really appreciated, and also reminded me why the course content was important. I hope to be an equine veterinarian and surgeon someday. My studies in Biomedical Science at UNH are giving me the foundation I need to succeed at veterinary school, and my classmates and professors have given me a community that I know I can always look to when my goals feel difficult to reach. title: Shaheen and DiLorenzo share thoughts on political issues as they fight for a spot in Congress - The New Hampshire
content: DURHAM- On Oct. 5, the University of New Hampshire (UNH) hosted the Carsey Candidate Policy Forum in the Memorial Union Building. Republican nominee Anthony DiLorenzo and Democratic nominee Stefany Shaheen were both given 35 minutes to share their opinions on what issues in New Hampshire are important to them and what their goals are if they were to win the election on November third. Stefany Shaheen at the Carsey Candidate Policy Forum The conversation was hosted by the Carsey School of Public Policy. The Forum is a nonpartisan series for congressional nominees in New Hampshire. The conversation was moderated by Kevin Sullivan, UNH Alum and a Washington Post Pulitzer Prize Winner. One of Shaheen's main topics was ending the war in Iran: “We're now seeing $4 gas prices; this wasn't a reality till this war started.” Shaheen says that she has heard from at least one person every day in the last two weeks worrying about gas prices this winter. Shaheen wants to see this war come to an end, and points out the soldiers that have been lost through its duration. “We've got to bring an end to this war, and Congress can do it,” Shaheen says. DiLorenzo comments on the fact that “we can not be the world's police officers.”  He says he is not “for boots on the ground” in this war and doesn't support the fact that the Iranian government should have nuclear weapons. DiLorenzo finds it strange that an oil-producing country would need to produce nuclear energy, but he says that foreign policy is not at the top of his priority list. Anthony DiLorenzo at the Carsey Candidate Policy Forum When the topic of artificial intelligence was brought up, Shaheen expressed concerns. “We should be focused on innovation that lifts everyone up, not wipes everyone out,” Shaheen says. She urges Washington to put up guardrails. DiLorenzo points out that there is good and bad in all technology. While it can be scary and unknown, he trusts the experts when they say it's containable. He does agree with his opponent that there needs to be guardrails added “to ensure privacy is protected.” Throughout the debate, Shaheen comments on DiLorenzo's support of President Donald Trump. Trump has endorsed DiLorenzo for the Congressional District race. On social media, Trump calls DiLorenzo a “very successful Businessman and Entrepreneur,” which is a point DiLorenzo uses during his campaign. “We need more business people in D.C.,” DiLorenzo says. He points out that he has worked since he was 8 years old and calls his opponent privileged due to their family. Shaheen then comments on how ICE has affected the state of New Hampshire. “This is not helping our community be safer,” Shaheen says. She mentions that the Department of Homeland Security shared that only 5% of people who are being detained have been charged with violent crimes. Shaheen speaks on hearing personal stories from families affected by ICE. DiLorenzo comments that we need immigration reform and that policies should reflect what the country needs. He believes that there is room for improvement; law enforcement needs more training and proper training. Both candidates agree that there is a housing issue in the Granite State. DiLorenzo comments on the high cost of infrastructure, but is still in favor of building. He comments on the fact that housing prices are outpacing wages. Shaheen makes a point of the tariffs' effect on our country. “Tariffs have wreaked havoc,” Shaheen says. She makes a statement claiming DiLorenzo’s support of these tariffs. She believes that they are hurting small businesses. Each candidate was given a minute to close. Shaheen declares that she is going to work hard for change in this country, and for its people’s support. “We have a choice between change or more of the same,” Shaheen says. She again highlights her opponent's support for the tariffs, war, and Trump. Shaheen speaks directly to UNH students, telling them to vote. “Don't let anyone tell you you're not allowed to vote.” DiLorenzo considers the election to be a “simple choice.” He calls Shaheen a “political insider who has come from a fairly privileged family,” and points out that the experience he brings is hard work and business. “We need more common sense business leadership in D.C. and less professional politicians, and that's why I'm running,” DiLorenzo says. With the election coming up, many are wondering what's next and who will win at the polls.

title: UNH falls to Monmouth on family weekend - The New Hampshire
content: The Monmouth Hawks traveled to take on the New Hampshire Wildcats on Oct. 17th. The Hawks weren't the only ones who traveled on Saturday. UNH also hosted its annual Family Weekend. title: Shannon Garvey: A UNH success story - The New Hampshire
content: In May of 2026, UNH English MFA (Master of Fine Arts) graduate Shannon Garvey received her first major publication with her novel, June Baby. Published and distributed by Random House and Thousand Voices Books, June Baby was a USA Today National Bestseller upon release, garnering acclaim from readers and critics alike. Bestselling author Coco Mellers describes the story as a “work of growing up” that is both “tender and precise,” with “Garvey’s prose [revealing] a writer of real emotional intelligence and depth.” The New York Times Book Review called the story an “old-fashioned love letter to summer romance, sun-fueled creativity and long rides on rusty bikes” — an “outsider’s story [that] unfolds in the voice of an insider.” Throughout our conversation, Garvey touched on what it has felt like to be propelled into literary success. In regards to the book tour she embarked on over the summer, she emphasized how “amazing [it was] to see [June Baby] connect with readers.” She goes on to say, “I spent four years writing it...I’m sure I would be nervous if I was talking about anything else in the world, but this is the one thing that I know best.” June Baby opens with seventeen year-old Ruth who, after losing her mother to cancer, leaves to live on a wealthy remote island with renowned photographer Diana Beckett. Ten years later, after tragedy upends her life again, Ruth must embark on a journey of mystery and self-discovery to reexamine everything she thought she knew about her past. It’s a coming-of-age story that explores both love and grief, embracing the duality between loss and possibility in one’s life. Describing her process, Garvey says that “writing a novel is such an experience, in empathy and curiosity; every day, curious to see where the story is going to lead and exercising this really beautiful empathy for characters that might not exist, but you are, every second, wondering how it might feel to be them in this scenario.” Garvey then discusses her emotional and physical attachment to a specific place, and how that manifested through her characters. “With Ruth, I was really interested in writing about somebody who was in love with a place, so the book is set on Block Island, a very small island off of Rhode Island,” the state in which Garvey herself grew up. She states she has been “fascinated by Block Island since [she] was a child,” and, through her writing, has been enamoured with the question of “what somebody might do to hold onto a place that they love that much.” Garvey makes it clear that Ruth is not her, but some of Ruth’s “fears and thoughts about the world” are things Garvey has thought and felt at various points in her life. “These characters aren't people you know at all, but to write them, you are drawing on that reservoir of your own emotions and your own connections to others.” As impressive as her novel’s acclaim is for an author and their debut work, Garvey is not the only one ecstatic about her recent success. In fact, she began writing June Baby while studying in UNH’s English MFA program, where the book eventually flourished into her thesis. She details the process. “The MFA thesis has to be 150 pages, and it can either be a collection of short stories or a novel excerpt,” but the workshop-based program “is really built around short stories...I knew from the beginning that I wanted my thesis to be a novel because I wanted to have the opportunity to have incredible writers like Tom [Payne] and Ann Williams and Jaed Coffin have their eyes on it…I thought that would be really valuable.” Of her time in the MFA program, she says “that there’s something really special about being one around a group of people who are taking the same thing you are very seriously…there’s something really transformational about inhaling that much work.” According to writer, professor, and head of the MFA department Thomas Payne, “the MFA program in Creative Writing has graduated any number of stellar writers of poetry, fiction and memoir over our last 50 years as a nationally-known program. But for Shannon to rocket out of UNH onto the Today show with basically her MFA thesis (this novel) a couple of years after graduating? That's just jaw dropping.” Garvey graduated in 2017 with a B.A. in Neuroscience and Behavior, and while in the MFA program, she taught undergraduate classes. These formative years provided her with an ever-deepening understanding of writing, literature, and what it means to find yourself through a work of art. Payne describes the “feeling” he had that Garvey was “going to hit a home run” after years of “knowing her fiction [and] seeing drafts of [June Baby].” In addition to June Baby’s popularity, Garvey has made a name for herself through her shorter works in the Saturday Evening Post and her feature on the Peabody-Award winning Moth Radio Hour. Now, after being on the “Today” show—which she considers to have been “incredibly surreal”—and in a variety of national magazines from Vogue to People, Garvey is well-underway on her second novel. “My way of dealing with the unknowns of this industry is always to be grateful for what has come to pass, and do the work every day…then, you know, we’ll see what happens.” Catch Shannon Garvey’s reading and Q&A for UNH’s Writer Series on Thursday, Oct. 22 at 5pm in Hamilton Smith Hall. The event was organized by Thomas Payne and the MFA department, and he hopes that “any UNH undergrad who wants to be a writer” comes to the event.

title: The Learning Landscape: The New England Agroforester - Fall Equinox 2026 - University of New Hampshire
content: ADAPT’s second Agroforestry Educator Cohort launched this July with a two-day immersive learning experience, gathering 13 educators from Vermont, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts. Beginning at Dartmouth College, Professor Theresa Ong and graduate student Krystal Bagnaschi introduced participants to key agroforestry concepts and shared the goals and vision of the ADAPT program. The group then toured several research and demonstration sites, including two food forests, the Experimental Linear Gap (ELG) research area, where a variety of forest farming crops are being studied, and an edible riparian buffer designed to support both ecological and food production goals. The riparian buffer was established in partnership with ReTreeUS, and Executive Director Richard Hodges joined the group to discuss food forest design and the organization's growing network of high school food forests throughout New England. On the second day, participants visited the Abenaki Garden in Hartford, Vermont, where Earl Hatley shared the story of the Community and Culture Acre, a teaching garden that also produces food and seeds for local food banks. Alongside the traditional Three Sisters planting, the site features hazelnuts, elderberries, ground cherries, and blueberries, with ongoing efforts to expand the area into a mature food forest system. The cohort concluded its field experience at Howling Wolf Farm in Randolph, Vermont, where Jenn Colby showcased her innovative approach to creating silvopasture through ecological succession. Participants learned how rotationally grazed sheep are integrated into the landscape, helping transform emerging woodlands into productive agroforestry systems while supporting animal welfare and ecosystem health. Looking ahead, both Cohort 1 and Cohort 2 participants will continue their field-based learning in Year 2 of the program. Upcoming visits include The Ecology School in Saco, Maine, on October 5 and the New Hampshire State Forest Nursery in Boscawen, NH, on November 13. For more information, contact State Coordinator Mike Smith at 4-H Community Agriculture and NH Ag in the Classroom. Two educators from the UNH Extension agroforestry program were recently featured on the Northeast Farm to School Collaborative's podcast, The Farm to School Podcast. Becky Denslow, a participant in the second Maple Tales cohort and now a member of the second ADAPT Agroforestry cohort, joined Mary Hartigan Demers, a member of the first ADAPT Agroforestry cohort, to share their experiences bringing agroforestry and maple education into their schools. The conversation highlights how educators are creating meaningful connections between students, trees, food systems, and local landscapes. Mary discusses developing a maple sugaring program at her middle school in downtown Manchester, and Becky reflects on her continuing agroforestry journey through multiple UNH Extension programs. An upcoming episode will feature Megan Glenn and other program leaders discussing the ADAPT Agroforestry program and cohorts, helping share lessons and successes from educators across the region. Listen to the episode on the Northeast Farm to School Collaborative's podcast page: The Farm to School Podcast. Members of the ADAPT Team participated in Erik Schellenberg's Temperate Syntropic Agroforestry webinar in August 2026. Drawing on his experience developing syntropic agroforestry systems in southern New York, Erik shared practical lessons, observations, and reflections from the field. Resources from the presentation include: Building on the introductory session, a second webinar on December 3, 2026 will take a deeper look at the theory, principles, and ecological relationships that underpin syntropic agroforestry. While some foundational concepts will be revisited, the session will be valuable for both those returning and those new to the approach. Participants are encouraged to bring questions about adapting syntropic practices to temperate climates. For more information, contact Jonathan Bates at Cornell Cooperative Extension. ReTreeUS Founder and Program Manager Richard Hodges prepares to plant a tree at a school site. Image credit: ReTreeUS. Discussions at the recent ADAPT all-hands meeting emphasized a challenge familiar to many agroforestry practitioners: how to establish educational plantings that remain productive, relevant, and well-maintained over time. ReTreeUS, a nonprofit organization working throughout New England, has spent the past 15 years developing and refining systems designed specifically to address those challenges in school settings. Founded by Richard Hodges, ReTreeUS began with a focus on helping schools create outdoor learning spaces centered around orchards and gardens. Over time, the organization found that long-term success depended not only on planting trees and gardens but also on developing practical approaches to maintenance, educator engagement, and curriculum integration. To date, ReTreeUS has helped establish more than 120 school and community orchards across Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, and Massachusetts. The organization originally set a goal of creating 100 school community orchards and has since expanded its focus to include school food forests. Over the next three years, the organization plans to establish 30 school food forests, including seven new sites this year. Foresters, farmers, technical advisors, service partners, and researchers observing tree plantings at a forest farming site at the ADAPT Project’s Fall 2026 All-Hands meeting. The ReTreeUS approach centers around systems that fit the realities of school operations. School gardens often face challenges related to summer maintenance, staff turnover, and weed management. To address these, ReTreeUS developed a "back-to-school garden" model. Schools receive trays of established crops such as lettuce and kale sourced from nearby farms. Students plant the seedlings in September, allowing gardens to become immediately productive while reducing summer maintenance demands. Cover crops help suppress weeds, improve soil health, and support pollinators during periods when students are not present. The organization's orchard model similarly prioritizes long-term stewardship. Typical school orchard plantings include 12 to 20 semi-dwarf fruit trees, often apples, pears, and peaches. ReTreeUS has developed deer-management strategies, planting protocols, and maintenance resources that schools can implement after installation. Teacher caretakers may receive stipends for ongoing stewardship, accompanied by progress reports and photographs documenting orchard development. Educational resources are another core component of the model. ReTreeUS provides standards-aligned lessons, presentations, videos, and enrichment materials that help teachers use orchards and food forests as living classrooms. By connecting outdoor spaces directly to existing curricula, orchards become more fully integrated into school operations and student learning. The organization's current food forest initiative expands on lessons learned through its orchard program. While each site is adapted to local conditions, plantings typically include multiple layers of perennial food-producing species. Fruit and nut trees may be combined with blueberries, raspberries, strawberries, grapevines, hazelnuts, perennial herbs, native plums, bush cherries, Cornelian cherries, and nitrogen-fixing species such as gomi. Clover is commonly seeded throughout the site as a living groundcover that suppresses weeds and contributes nitrogen to the system. One challenge ReTreeUS has worked to address is the perception that food forests are difficult to manage or appear untidy. School sites often require landscapes that are both ecologically functional and visually organized. Sheet mulching, straw, paper, defined planting zones, and groundcover establishment reduce competition from weeds while maintaining an appearance appropriate for educational campuses. Many of these plantings begin producing harvestable crops within the first year, particularly berries, herbs, and other perennial species. This early productivity helps sustain student interest while providing opportunities to explore topics such as food production, ecology, pollination, soil health, and agroforestry. Feedback from participating schools consistently highlights student engagement. Educators report that outdoor learning environments often create opportunities for students who may struggle in traditional classroom settings to participate in different ways. Planting, observing, harvesting, and caring for perennial systems allows students to engage directly with ecological processes over multiple seasons. For ADAPT partners exploring agroforestry in educational settings, the ReTreeUS model offers a practical example of how long-term stewardship, curriculum integration, and maintenance planning can support the success of school-based agroforestry projects. As interest in school food forests continues to grow across New England, these experiences provide useful insights into how agroforestry systems can become lasting educational and community assets. Civil Eats' Summer 2026 Food and Farming Book Guide hits several relevant themes for agroforestry in the Northeast: perennial agriculture, Indigenous ecological knowledge, soil health, environmental contamination, and community-led food systems. While the guide covers a wide range of topics, a handful of titles stand out for agroforestry practitioners, educators, and technical service providers. For New England agroforesters, these titles offer both practical insights and a broader perspective on the forces shaping the future of regenerative agriculture, conservation, and tree-based farming systems. Investors often turn to recommendations made by Wall Street analysts before making a Buy, Sell, or Hold decision about a stock. While media reports about rating changes by these brokerage-firm employed (or sell-side) analysts often affect a stock's price, do they really matter? Let's take a look at what these Wall Street heavyweights have to say about UnitedHealth Group (UNH) before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage. UnitedHealth currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.54, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by 27 brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.54 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy. Of the 27 recommendations that derive the current ABR, 18 are Strong Buy and three are Buy. Strong Buy and Buy respectively account for 66.7% and 11.1% of all recommendations. According to several studies, brokerage recommendations have little to no success guiding investors to choose stocks with the most potential for price appreciation. Are you wondering why? The vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover often results in a strong positive bias of their analysts in rating it. Our research shows that for every "Strong Sell" recommendation, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations. This means that the interests of these institutions are not always aligned with those of retail investors, giving little insight into the direction of a stock's future price movement. It would therefore be best to use this information to validate your own analysis or a tool that has proven to be highly effective at predicting stock price movements. Zacks Rank, our proprietary stock rating tool with an impressive externally audited track record, categorizes stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), and is an effective indicator of a stock's price performance in the near future. Therefore, using the ABR to validate the Zacks Rank could be an efficient way of making a profitable investment decision. Although both Zacks Rank and ABR are displayed in a range of 1--5, they are different measures altogether. Broker recommendations are the sole basis for calculating the ABR, which is typically displayed in decimals (such as 1.28). The Zacks Rank, on the other hand, is a quantitative model designed to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5. It has been and continues to be the case that analysts employed by brokerage firms are overly optimistic with their recommendations. Because of their employers' vested interests, these analysts issue more favorable ratings than their research would support, misguiding investors far more often than helping them. On the other hand, earnings estimate revisions are at the core of the Zacks Rank. And empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements. Furthermore, the different grades of the Zacks Rank are applied proportionately across all stocks for which brokerage analysts provide earnings estimates for the current year. In other words, at all times, this tool maintains a balance among the five ranks it assigns. Another key difference between the ABR and Zacks Rank is freshness. The ABR is not necessarily up-to-date when you look at it. But, since brokerage analysts keep revising their earnings estimates to account for a company's changing business trends, and their actions get reflected in the Zacks Rank quickly enough, it is always timely in indicating future price movements. In terms of earnings estimate revisions for UnitedHealth, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the current year has increased 4% over the past month to $20.52. Analysts' growing optimism over the company's earnings prospects, as indicated by strong agreement among them in revising EPS estimates higher, could be a legitimate reason for the stock to soar in the near term. title: SHARPP hosts annual 'Take Back the Night' event - The New Hampshire
content: On the night of Thursday Oct. 15, on the Thompson Hall lawn at the University of New Hampshire, the SHARPP Center for Interpersonal Violence Awareness, Prevention, and Advocacy hosted its annual Take Back the Night (TBTN) event, an event that has been hosted since 1981. TBTN is an awareness event for victims of interpersonal violence. The event calls people to action and holds a vigil. While some attendees were wrapping chilled hands around warm cups of apple cider, tea, or hot chocolate provided by UNH catering, others were busy creating posters with encouraging messages reminding people they are never alone. “This event is important, it’s showing campus how interpersonal violence affects campus, and it gives survivors a place to speak and be heard where they otherwise aren't able to be,” said Rachel Stewart, the director of SHARPP. As the event opened, every attendee was given a glowstick which was later used in an activity to show how every person at the event had been impacted by interpersonal violence, either directly or indirectly. UNH Acapella group, The New Hampshire Notables have performed at the past three TBTN events. This year they chose to perform the song “Can't Catch Me Now” by Olivia Rodrigo, to highlight the struggle and resilience of interpersonal violence survivors. Their contribution was a moment of calm to help attendees transition into the open mic segment of the event. At the start of the open mic, Stewart briefly mentioned recent events at Cornell University involving interpersonal violence, highlighting its ubiquitous nature on college campuses. The event then moved into the speaker portion of the open mic. “I want people to know that this community is for them,” said Darian Kavlahao, one of the event MCs for TBTN. Many attendees got the opportunity to either speak or listen to the stories of others, sharing awareness and creating a supportive and inclusive environment. “[Interpersonal violence] is a part of my story, but it is not the whole story.” said Emma Schmidl-Gagne, a community advisor for SHARPP and the other event MC. While many were sharing their stories, each attendee was also given a candle that was lit and held for the remainder of the event. As the event ended with many feeling less alone, Stewart reminds all that this does not end here. “This event is great, but it can't just be one night. Everyone needs to care about interpersonal violence, it has to be every day,” Stewart said. SHARPP Center resources are available for all. The SHARPP Center is located on the 3rd Floor of Smith Hall. Resources include scheduling a meeting or contacting the SHARPP office at (603) 862- 3494. SHARPP also has a 24/7 helpline at (603) 862-7233. Drop-in hours have been temporarily paused for Fall 2026 due to staffing constraints. However, you can still stop by or contact SHARPP to make a virtual or in-person appointment. The SHARPP Center offers confidential appointments and a safe space to meet with staff and representatives.

title: Learning Curve - University of New Hampshire
content: These experiences, and many more, await the undergraduates who venture beyond the classroom to conduct their own research. They learn by doing, gain access to sophisticated tools, and forge distinctive relationships with faculty mentors. The work can be surprising, disgusting, challenging — but it’s always enlightening and, for most, transformative. UNH, as a public research institution with a roll-up-our-sleeves, git ’er done ethic that drives innovation and problem-solving, stokes the curiosity of these nascent explorers with opportunities galore. This exceptional commitment to undergraduate research results in nearly 2,000 students presenting at the annual Undergraduate Research Conference, one of the nation’s largest. Read on to meet some student researchers funded by the Hamel Center for Undergraduate Research, whose passion for discovery is leading them to real-world skills — and solutions. Mentor: Nathan Furey, associate professor of biological sciences Research: Identification of River Herring Predators in the Bellamy River “I started looking for opportunities during my freshman year and have been working with Dr. Furey ever since. My experience conducting undergraduate research has been full of cool discoveries, interesting challenges, and lots of time out in the field. [I remember] sitting on a little island in the middle of the Bellamy River on my first photo download day, nervous about not seeing anything on the cameras, and immediately opening to a photo of a great blue heron with a river herring in its beak. This was exactly what we were hoping to find!” Mentor: Otto Luna, digital resources curator, art and art history “I have been able to do archival research on art pieces as well as dive deeply into art provenance and how it impacts cultural heritage. As I’m looking toward the future, I hope to use my research skills and knowledge gained during this experience to break into the small field of art conservation in public art institutions. Being able to do under-graduate research also prepares me for master’s programs and better fills out my undergraduate resume of skills.” Mentor: Dante Scala, professor of political science and international affairs Research: Intraparty Ideological Conflict: A Case Study of the 2026 NH-01 Primary Elections “I am conducting interviews with candidates, visiting campaign events, studying political science literature, and conducting textual analyses of candidates’ policy statements. It has been an incredible privilege to be able to meet candidates in person and speak to them directly. This has been the best and most unique part of the project. It adds a human element to the other more technical and theoretical aspects of the project.” Program of study: marine, estuarine, and freshwater biology and sustainability Mentor: Nathan Furey, associate professor of biological sciences Research: Investigating Diets of Striped Bass and Atlantic Cod and the Energy Content of Their Prey “This experience has been much more broad than I was expecting because our lab is so collaborative. My favorite part of this experience was working with New Hampshire Fish and Game on its bag seine survey to collect fish samples for the prey energy density portion of my study. I enjoyed cruising around the bay, wading through varying levels of muddy substrate, and the excitement of seeing what cool fish we caught in the net. All of these hands-on experiences will definitely help me succeed in the future as I am now familiar with many different fisheries-related techniques.” Program of study: music performance; neuroscience and behavior Mentors: David Upham, associate professor of music education, and Kate Christison-Lagay, assistant professor of biological sciences Research: Emotional Responsiveness to Western Classical Music in Musicians versus Non-Musicians (with Tara Saran '27 and Nicole Di Benedetto '27) “A standout moment was when we first unboxed our pupillometer (the device for measuring pupil size) in my professor's lab. The whole team was there, and it was super exciting to see the device we had been discussing for months actually in the lab. It was also really exciting when we had our first participant in the lab and saw our program being used and heard their thoughts on the music after all of the work that built up to it.” Mentor: Casey Roark, assistant professor of psychology Research: Categorization Comparing Gamified and Traditional Conditions Provided Physically or Digitally “I have always loved asking questions about the world around me. This experience gave me a look into what being a researcher means and how to problem-solve when conducting my own study.” Mentors: Sajay Arthanat, professor of occupational therapy, and Marguerite Corvini, clinical assistant professor and director of simulation and digital health Research: An Innovative Virtual Reality-Based Peer Wellness Program for Rural Care Providers I have gained both technical knowledge and experience through my research, but most importantly I have seen how research affects people firsthand. Even before I had the true, numerical results, I could see how what I was doing was changing lives.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.
